Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. President Trump today said he's considering
a trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin. It comes

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the subject of the trilateral meeting had come

to a Wall Street Journal report that Putin had suggested the meeting with Trump and Xi
to work out a settlement to the war in Ukraine acceptable to Moscow. NPR has not independently

The Supreme Court has declined to revive plea deals for the alleged mastermind of the September
11 terror attacks, Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two of his co-defendants. That means three
men, who are being held at a U.S. military prison in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, could continue
to proceed toward a death penalty trial. NPR's Sasha Pfeiffer reports.
Plea deals with these men were announced about two years ago and would have let them plead
guilty and get up to life in prison rather than risk being put to death. But former Defense
Secretary Lloyd Austin immediately retracted the agreements. And now, the last opportunity
for the defendants to appeal that decision has come to an end.
The 9/11 case has been dragging on for so long that many Guantanamo lawyers think the
only way to resolve it is with plea deals. But this Supreme Court order puts the case
back on track to be tried. The trial's tentative start date is June 2028, but ongoing legal
hurdles could cause even more delays. Sasha Pfeiffer, NPR News.
What began as a strike by high school students and teachers in a Parisian suburb has ballooned
into nationwide protests and in many cases destructive riots across France. Dominique
Moisey is a political scientist and senior adviser at the Think Tank Institute Montaigne.
He has more on why this escalated.
Well, I think the encounter between the violence of those who were there, not to demonstrate,
but to break the Republic or to benefit from the shops they would steal from and the inefficiency
at the end of the measures taken by the police. And so that's a real major problem, especially
for a country like France.
Officials have imposed curfews in parts of the country and Europe index stock indexes
fell more than one percent following the protests. This is NPR News from Washington.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck Yemeni government forces with missiles killing at least 53 soldiers
at a military camp. The attack was one of the deadliest strikes since a resurgence in
fighting in Yemen this summer. The fighting between the Houthis and Yemen's Saudi-backed
government forces is widening is a widening front in the Iran war that began in February.
Ireland is a tech hub in Europe, with Dublin home to the European headquarters of Meta,
Google and Microsoft. The Irish government touted ways that AI can make Europe more competitive
at an AI conference last week. Meanwhile, as NPR's Willow Rubin reports, former tech
workers staged a counter-summit to voice their AI concerns.
The thesis of this counter-summit can be summed up in a t-shirt worn by former tech worker
Bruna Becista Nicochelli. It's a picture of two people, all pixelated, smashing a computer.
And it says workers against Slopaganda. Slop, AI slop, and aganda, propaganda. People
here say AI is transforming the workplace so fast it could make jobs worse, replace
jobs, make people dumber. They talk solutions, like workers having a voice in management's
decisions about how and why they're using AI. They're also suggesting a four-day work
week. The union is bringing these ideas to the next Irish parliamentary subcommittee
meeting on AI. Willow Rubin, NPR News, Dublin.
Christiane Amanpour will be leaving CNN after 43 years. The network's longtime anchor will
end her show on CNN International in May. The 68-year-old will also end her PBS show,
Amanpour and Company at year's end. Her exit comes as CNN has a new owner, Skydance, bringing
it under the same roof as CBS. This is NPR.
